**Original Question:**
Between the top 5 countries on the Heritage Foundation's Index of Economic Freedom by Government Spending, which one has the highest level of caution in their Travel Advisory according to the U.S. Department of State as of February 2024? Exclude Sudan, Venezuela, Iran, and Lebanon from your analysis.

**Previous Reasoning Steps:**
[turn 1] We need: Top 5 countries on Heritage Index of Economic Freedom by Government Spending. Then find which has highest level of caution in their Travel Advisory according to U.S. Dept of State as of Feb 2024. Exclude Sudan, Venezuela, Iran, Lebanon. So likely top 5 are some countries. Need to confirm list and travel advisory categories (Level 0: Normal, 1: Exercise Increased Caution, 2: Reconsider Travel, 3: Do Not Travel). Highest level of caution = highest category number.

We must provide answer citing sources.

Plan: Search Heritage Index top 5 in that metric. Then search U.S. Dept State travel advisory level for those countries. Identify highest caution.

Thus two sources: Heritage Index and U.S. Dept State. Could use web_fetch for each.

Let's search.

[turn 2] We need top 5 countries on the Heritage Foundation's Index of Economic Freedom by Government Spending. Actually index is by government spending? Might be a specific sub-index. The query gave top rankings overall. But question says by Government Spending, so likely a sub-category ranking. We need top 5 countries on that sub-index. Then among those, find which has highest level of caution in their Travel Advisory according to US Department of State as of Feb 2024. Exclude Sudan, Venezuela, Iran, Lebanon (not likely in top 5 anyway). So determine top 5 by Government Spending. Let's search.

[turn 3] We have top 5 countries by Government Spending from Heritage Index. But we need the top 5 countries on the Heritage Foundation's Index of Economic Freedom by Government Spending? Actually “by Government Spending” indicates there may be a sub-index for government spending. Heritage publishes "Index of Economic Freedom by Government Spending" as a category ranking. Need top 5 of that list. Then excluding Sudan, Venezuela, Iran, Lebanon. Among remaining, find which has highest level of caution in their Travel Advisory as of February 2024 by U.S. Department of State. Travel advisory levels: Level 1 (exercise normal precautions), Level 2 (exercise increased caution), Level 3 (reconsider travel), Level 4 (do not travel). Highest level of caution means Level 4 is highest? Probably. So find which country among those top 5 has Level 4 advisory as of Feb 2024.

We need to know those top 5.

Government safety warning for foreign travel

A **travel warning**, **travel alert**, or **travel advisory** is an official [warning statement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precautionary_statement "Precautionary statement") issued by [government agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_agency "Government agency") to provide information about the relative safety of [travelling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel "Travel") to or visiting one or more specific foreign [countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country "Country") or destinations.[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel_advisory#cite_note-1) The purpose is to enable travelers to make an informed decision about a particular travel destination, and to help travellers prepare adequately for what may be encountered on their trip. In the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), travel warnings are issued by the [Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State") and are often called warden messages.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel_advisory#cite_note-USDoS-2)[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel_advisory#cite_note-3)

Travel advisories may relate to issues such as [inclement weather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inclement_weather "Inclement weather"), [security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security "Security") matters, [civil unrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_unrest "Civil unrest") or [disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disease "Disease").[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel_advisory#cite_note-4)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [Travel advisory](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Travel_advisory&redirect=no "Travel advisory"))

Government safety warning for foreign travel

A **travel warning**, **travel alert**, or **travel advisory** is an official [warning statement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precautionary_statement "Precautionary statement") issued by [government agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_agency "Government agency") to provide information about the relative safety of [travelling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel "Travel") to or visiting one or more specific foreign [countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country "Country") or destinations.[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel_advisory#cite_note-1) The purpose is to enable travelers to make an informed decision about a particular travel destination, and to help travellers prepare adequately for what may be encountered on their trip. In the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), travel warnings are issued by the [Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State") and are often called warden messages.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel_advisory#cite_note-USDoS-2)[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel_advisory#cite_note-3)

Travel advisories may relate to issues such as [inclement weather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inclement_weather "Inclement weather"), [security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security "Security") matters, [civil unrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_unrest "Civil unrest") or [disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disease "Disease").[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel_advisory#cite_note-4)

The **United Arab Emirates** (**UAE**),[[b]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-15) also known simply as the **Emirates**,[[c]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-16) is a country in [West Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Asia "West Asia"), situated at the eastern end of the [Arabian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula "Arabian Peninsula"). It is a [federal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_monarchy "Federal monarchy") semi-constitutional [monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy "Monarchy") made up of [seven emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirates_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "Emirates of the United Arab Emirates"), with [Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi") serving as its national capital. The UAE borders [Oman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oman "Oman") to the east and northeast, and [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") to the south and southwest. It shares [maritime borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_boundary "Maritime boundary") with Saudi Arabia, [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar"), and [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") in the [Persian Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf"), and with Oman in the [Gulf of Oman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Oman "Gulf of Oman"). In 2024, the UAE had an estimated population of over 11 million. [Dubai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai "Dubai") is the country's [largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_the_United_Arab_Emirates "List of cities in the United Arab Emirates"). [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") is the [state religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_religion "State religion"). [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic "Arabic") is the official language while [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") remains the most spoken language and the language of business.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-Siemund-2)[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-17)

The present-day United Arab Emirates is located within the historical region of [Eastern Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Arabia "Eastern Arabia"), which was oriented to [maritime trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_trade "Maritime trade") and [seafaring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seafaring "Seafaring"). The [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire") arrived in the region around 1500 and set up bases on the territory while waging [wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese%E2%80%93Safavid_wars "Portuguese–Safavid wars") against the [Persians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safavid_Iran "Safavid Iran"). By the 19th century, with [pearling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearling_industry "Pearling industry") becoming a major economic activity, [piracy became rampant in the gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piracy_in_the_Persian_Gulf "Piracy in the Persian Gulf"), prompting [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") intervention.[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-bandits-18)[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-:11-19) Local [sheikhdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikhdoms "Sheikhdoms") formed a pact with the United Kingdom to create the [Trucial States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trucial_States "Trucial States"), a [British protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_protectorate "British protectorate") that was effectively shielded from attempted [Saudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Saudi_state "First Saudi state") and [Omani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omani_Empire "Omani Empire")[suzerainty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzerainty "Suzerainty").[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-20) The Trucial States remained under British influence until full independence as the United Arab Emirates in 1971. [Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_bin_Sultan_Al_Nahyan "Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan"), ruler of Abu Dhabi and the country's first president (1971–2004), oversaw rapid development of the Emirates by investing revenues from newly found [oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_reserve "Oil reserve") into [healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_care "Health care"), [education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education "Education"), and [infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure "Infrastructure").[[18]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-21)

The United Arab Emirates is considered a [middle power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_power "Middle power") in global affairs;[[19]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-22) Dubai serves as an international hub of finance, tourism, and commerce.[[20]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-:9-23)[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-24) Only 11% of the population are native [Emiratis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emiratis "Emiratis"); the vast majority of inhabitants are [expatriates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expatriates "Expatriates") and [migrant workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migrant_workers "Migrant workers"), most of whom are from [South Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia").[[22]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-25) The UAE has the world's [seventh-largest oil reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_proven_oil_reserves "List of countries by proven oil reserves") and [seventh-largest natural gas reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_natural_gas_proven_reserves "List of countries by natural gas proven reserves").[[23]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-EIA-26)[[24]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-27) The UAE has the most diversified economy among the members of the [Gulf Cooperation Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Cooperation_Council "Gulf Cooperation Council") (GCC), having become less reliant on natural resources in the 21st century and increasingly focusing on tourism and business.[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-28) The UAE is a member of the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations"), [Arab League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_League "Arab League"), [Organisation of Islamic Cooperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_Islamic_Cooperation "Organisation of Islamic Cooperation"), [Non-Aligned Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement "Non-Aligned Movement"), [World Trade Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Organization "World Trade Organization"), and [BRICS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRICS "BRICS"); it is also a dialogue partner of the [Shanghai Cooperation Organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Cooperation_Organisation "Shanghai Cooperation Organisation").

The [Federal Supreme Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Supreme_Council "Federal Supreme Council"), made up of the seven ruling [emirs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirs "Emirs"), is the highest state authority. It jointly appoints one member as [federal president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "President of the United Arab Emirates"), who appoints a [prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_prime_ministers_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "List of prime ministers of the United Arab Emirates"), who forms and leads [the cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "Cabinet of the United Arab Emirates").[[26]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-29) The UAE is an [authoritarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarianism "Authoritarianism") state but generally liberal by regional standards.[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-:11-19) It ranks highly in several social indicators such as housing, [healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_the_United_Arab_Emirates "Healthcare in the United Arab Emirates"), [education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_the_United_Arab_Emirates "Education in the United Arab Emirates") and personal safety, as well as the highest regionally in the [Human Development Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Development_Index "Human Development Index").[[27]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-30) Human rights organisations consider the UAE substandard on human rights, ranking low in the [human freedom index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Freedom_Index "Human Freedom Index") due to reports of government critics being imprisoned and tortured, families harassed by the state security apparatus, and cases of [forced disappearances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_disappearance "Forced disappearance").[[28]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-31) Individual rights such as the freedoms of [assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_assembly "Freedom of assembly"), [association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_association "Freedom of association"), [expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_expression "Freedom of expression"), and the [freedom of the press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Press_Freedom_Index "Press Freedom Index") are severely repressed.[[29]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-32)

## Etymology

The United Arab Emirates is named after the seven emirates that formed a federation: the Emirate of [Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi"), the Emirate of [Dubai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai "Dubai"), the Emirate of [Ajman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajman "Ajman"), the Emirate of [Sharjah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharjah "Sharjah"), the Emirate of [Ras Al Khaimah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah "Ras Al Khaimah"), the Emirate of [Umm Al Quwain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umm_Al_Quwain "Umm Al Quwain"), and the Emirate of [Fujairah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujairah "Fujairah").[[30]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-33)

## History

Main article: [History of the United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "History of the United Arab Emirates")

### Antiquity

[![Image 15](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/C%C3%A1ntaro_%2826738115330%29.jpg/250px-C%C3%A1ntaro_%2826738115330%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:C%C3%A1ntaro_(26738115330).jpg)

2nd century [BCE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era "Common Era") era jar found in [Mleiha Archaeological site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mleiha_Archaeological_Centre "Mleiha Archaeological Centre") in Sharjah

Stone tools recovered reveal a settlement of people from Africa some 127,000 years ago and a stone tool used for butchering animals discovered on the Arabian coast suggests an even older habitation from 130,000 years ago.[[31]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-34) In time, lively trading links developed with civilisations in [Mesopotamia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesopotamia "Mesopotamia"), Iran, and the [Harappan culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_Valley_civilisation "Indus Valley civilisation") of the Indus Valley. This contact persisted and became wider, probably motivated by the trade in copper from the [Hajar Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajar_Mountains "Hajar Mountains"), which commenced around 3,000 BCE.[[32]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-35) Sumerian sources talk of the [Magan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magan_(civilization) "Magan (civilization)") civilisation, which has been identified as encompassing the modern UAE and Oman.[[33]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-36)

There are six periods of human settlement with distinctive behaviours in the region before Islam, which include the [Hafit period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafit_period "Hafit period") from 3,200 to 2,600 BCE, the [Umm Al Nar culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umm_Al_Nar_culture "Umm Al Nar culture") from 2,600 to 2,000 BCE, and the [Wadi Suq culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wadi_Suq_culture "Wadi Suq culture") from 2,000 to 1,300 BCE. From 1,200 BCE to the advent of Islam in Eastern Arabia, through three distinctive [Iron Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age_in_the_United_Arab_Emirates "Iron Age in the United Arab Emirates") and the [Mleiha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mleiha "Mleiha") period, the area was variously occupied by the [Achaemenids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire "Achaemenid Empire") and other forces, and saw the construction of fortified settlements and extensive husbandry thanks to the development of the [_falaj_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qanat "Qanat") irrigation system.

### Islam

The spread of [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") to the northeastern tip of the [Arabian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula "Arabian Peninsula") is thought to have followed directly from a letter sent by the [Islamic prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_prophet "Islamic prophet")[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") to the rulers of [Oman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oman "Oman") in 630 CE. This led to a group of rulers travelling to [Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina "Medina"), converting to Islam, and subsequently driving a successful uprising against the unpopular [Sassanids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasanian_Empire "Sasanian Empire"), who dominated the coast at the time.[[34]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeard-Bey1996127-37) Following the death of Muhammad, the new Islamic communities south of the [Persian Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf") threatened to disintegrate, with insurrections against the [Muslim leaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_leaders "Muslim leaders"). Caliph [Abu Bakr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Bakr "Abu Bakr") sent an army from the capital Medina which completed its reconquest of the territory ([the Ridda Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridda_wars "Ridda wars")) with the [Battle of Dibba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dibba "Battle of Dibba") in which 10,000 lives are thought to have been lost.[[35]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeard-Bey1996127%E2%80%93128-38) This assured the integrity of the [Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate "Caliphate") and the unification of the Arabian Peninsula under the newly emerging [Rashidun Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashidun_Caliphate "Rashidun Caliphate").

In 637, Julfar—situated within the geographic boundaries of modern-day [Ras Al Khaimah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah "Ras Al Khaimah")—was an important port that was used as a staging post for the Islamic invasion of the [Sasanian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasanian_Empire "Sasanian Empire").[[36]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-AbedHellyer2001-39) The area of the [Al Ain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Ain "Al Ain")/[Buraimi Oasis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buraimi_Oasis "Buraimi Oasis") was known as Tu'am and was an important trading post for camel routes between the coast and the Arabian interior.[[37]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeard-Bey199622%E2%80%9323-40)

The earliest [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") site in the UAE was first discovered in the 1990s, an extensive monastic complex on what is now known as [Sir Bani Yas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Bani_Yas "Sir Bani Yas") Island and which dates back to the seventh century. Thought to be [Nestorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nestorianism "Nestorianism") and built in 600 CE, the church appears to have been abandoned peacefully in 750 CE.[[38]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-41) It forms a rare physical link to a legacy of Christianity, which is thought to have spread across the peninsula from 50 to 350 CE following trade routes. Certainly, by the fifth century, Oman had a bishop named John – the last bishop of Oman being Etienne, in 676 CE.[[39]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-42)

### Portuguese era

[![Image 16](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Forte_de_doba.jpg/250px-Forte_de_doba.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Forte_de_doba.jpg)

A painting of the [Portuguese Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire")[Doba Fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doba_Fortress?action=edit&redlink=1 "Doba Fortress (page does not exist)")[[pt](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forte%20de%20Doba "pt:Forte de Doba")] in [Dibba Al-Hisn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dibba_Al-Hisn "Dibba Al-Hisn") in 1620

The harsh desert environment led to the emergence of the "versatile tribesman", nomadic groups who subsisted due to a variety of economic activities, including animal husbandry, agriculture, and hunting. The seasonal movements of these groups led not only to frequent clashes between groups but also to the establishment of seasonal and semi-seasonal settlements and centres. These formed tribal groupings whose names are still carried by modern Emiratis, including the [Bani Yas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bani_Yas "Bani Yas") and [Al Bu Falah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Nahyan_family "Al Nahyan family") of [Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi"), Al Ain, [Liwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liwa_Oasis "Liwa Oasis"), and the west coast; the [Dhawahir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhawahir "Dhawahir"), Awamir, [Al Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Ali_(tribe) "Al Ali (tribe)"), and [Manasir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manasir_(tribe) "Manasir (tribe)") of the interior; the [Sharqiyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharqiyin "Sharqiyin") of the east coast; and the [Qawasim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qasimi "Al-Qasimi") to the north.[[40]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-43)

With the expansion of European [colonial empires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_empire "Colonial empire"), [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire"), [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire"), and [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Empire "Dutch Empire") forces appeared in the Persian Gulf region. By the 18th century, the Bani Yas confederation was the dominant force in most of the area now known as Abu Dhabi,[[41]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeard-Bey199643-44)[[42]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-45)[[43]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-46) while the Northern [Al Qawasim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qasimi "Al-Qasimi") (Al Qasimi) dominated maritime commerce. The Portuguese maintained an influence over the coastal settlements, building [forts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortification "Fortification") in the wake of the bloody 16th-century conquests of coastal communities by [Albuquerque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque "Afonso de Albuquerque") and the Portuguese commanders who followed him – particularly on the east coast at [Muscat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscat "Muscat"), [Sohar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sohar "Sohar"), and [Khor Fakkan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khor_Fakkan "Khor Fakkan").[[44]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeard-Bey1996282-47)

The southern coast of the Persian Gulf was known to the British as the "[Pirate Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "History of the United Arab Emirates")",[[45]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-48)[[46]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-49) as boats of the Al Qawasim federation harassed British-flagged shipping from the 17th century into the 19th.[[47]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-50) The charge of piracy is disputed by modern Emirati historians, including the current ruler of Sharjah, [Sheikh Sultan Al Qasimi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_bin_Muhammad_Al-Qasimi "Sultan bin Muhammad Al-Qasimi"), in his 1986 book _The Myth of Arab Piracy in the Gulf_.[[48]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-51)

[![Image 17](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Persian_Gulf_1507-1750.gif/250px-Persian_Gulf_1507-1750.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Persian_Gulf_1507-1750.gif)

Purple – [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire") in the Persian Gulf in the 16th and 17th century. Main cities, ports, and routes.

[![Image 18](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Ras_Al_Khaimah_under_attack%2C_1809_01.jpg/250px-Ras_Al_Khaimah_under_attack%2C_1809_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ras_Al_Khaimah_under_attack,_1809_01.jpg)

A painting depicting the burning of the coastal town and port of [Emirate of Ras Al Khaimah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Ras_Al_Khaimah "Emirate of Ras Al Khaimah") during the [Persian Gulf campaign of 1809](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf_campaign_of_1809 "Persian Gulf campaign of 1809")

British expeditions to protect their Indian trade routes led to campaigns against Ras Al Khaimah and other harbours along the coast, including the [Persian Gulf campaign of 1809](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf_campaign_of_1809 "Persian Gulf campaign of 1809") and the more successful [campaign of 1819](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf_campaign_of_1819 "Persian Gulf campaign of 1819"). The following year, Britain and a number of local rulers signed a [maritime truce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Maritime_Treaty_of_1820 "General Maritime Treaty of 1820"),[[49]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-52) giving rise to the term [Trucial States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trucial_States "Trucial States"), which came to define the status of the coastal emirates. A further treaty was signed in 1843 and in 1853, the [Perpetual Maritime Truce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetual_Maritime_Truce "Perpetual Maritime Truce") was agreed. To this was added the 'Exclusive Agreements', signed in 1892, which made the Trucial States a British protectorate.[[50]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-53)

Under the 1892 treaty, the trucial sheikhs agreed not to dispose of any territory except to the British and not to enter into relationships with any foreign government other than the British without their consent. In return, the British promised to protect the Trucial Coast from all aggression by sea and to help in case of land attack. British maritime policing meant that pearling fleets could operate in relative security. However, the British prohibition of the [slave trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_slavery "History of slavery") meant an important source of income was lost to some sheikhs and merchants.[[51]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-54)

In 1869, the Qubaisat tribe settled at [Khor Al Adaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khor_Al_Adaid "Khor Al Adaid") and tried to enlist the support of the Ottomans. Khor Al Adaid was claimed by Abu Dhabi at that time, a claim supported by the British. In 1906, the British Political Resident, [Percy Cox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Cox "Percy Cox"), confirmed in writing to the ruler of Abu Dhabi, [Zayed bin Khalifa Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_bin_Khalifa_Al_Nahyan "Zayed bin Khalifa Al Nahyan") ('Zayed the Great'), that Khor Al Adaid belonged to his sheikhdom.[[52]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-55)

### British era and discovery of oil

See also: [Persian Gulf campaign of 1809](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf_campaign_of_1809 "Persian Gulf campaign of 1809"), [Persian Gulf campaign of 1819](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf_campaign_of_1819 "Persian Gulf campaign of 1819"), [General Maritime Treaty of 1820](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Maritime_Treaty_of_1820 "General Maritime Treaty of 1820"), and [Trucial States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trucial_States "Trucial States")

[![Image 19](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Dhayah_Fort_showing_hilltop_location.jpg/250px-Dhayah_Fort_showing_hilltop_location.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dhayah_Fort_showing_hilltop_location.jpg)

[Dhayah Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhayah_Fort "Dhayah Fort") at the hill top. In 1819 it was the last [Al-Qasimi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qasimi "Al-Qasimi") stronghold to fall in the [Persian Gulf campaign of 1819](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf_campaign_of_1819 "Persian Gulf campaign of 1819"). The fall of Dhayah was to pave the way for the signing of the [General Maritime Treaty of 1820](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Maritime_Treaty_of_1820 "General Maritime Treaty of 1820").

During the 19th and early 20th centuries, the [pearling industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_hunting "Pearl hunting") thrived, providing both income and employment to the people of the Persian Gulf.[[53]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-56) The [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") had a severe impact on the industry, but it was the [economic depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_depression "Economic depression") of the late 1920s and early 1930s, coupled with the invention of the [cultured pearl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultured_pearl "Cultured pearl"), that wiped out the trade. The remnants of the trade eventually faded away shortly after the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), when the newly independent [Government of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India "Government of India") imposed heavy taxation on imported pearls. The decline of pearling resulted in extreme economic hardship in the Trucial States.[[54]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-57)

In 1922, the British government secured undertakings from the rulers of the Trucial States not to sign concessions with foreign companies without their consent. Aware of the potential for the development of natural resources such as oil, following finds in Persia (from 1908) and Mesopotamia (from 1927), a British-led oil company, the [Iraq Petroleum Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_Petroleum_Company "Iraq Petroleum Company") (IPC), showed an interest in the region. The [Anglo-Persian Oil Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Persian_Oil_Company "Anglo-Persian Oil Company") (APOC, later to become [British Petroleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BP "BP"), or BP) had a 23.75% share in IPC. From 1935, onshore concessions to explore for oil were granted by local rulers, with APOC signing the first one on behalf of Petroleum Concessions Ltd (PCL), an associate company of IPC.[[55]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-58)

APOC was prevented from developing the region alone because of the restrictions of the [Red Line Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_Agreement "Red Line Agreement"), which required it to operate through IPC. A number of options between PCL and the trucial rulers were signed, providing useful revenue for communities experiencing poverty following the collapse of the pearl trade. However, the wealth of oil which the rulers could see from the revenues accruing to surrounding countries remained elusive. The first bore holes in Abu Dhabi were drilled by IPC's operating company, Petroleum Development (Trucial Coast) Ltd (PDTC) at Ras Sadr in 1950, with a 13,000-foot-deep (4,000-metre) bore hole taking a year to drill and turning out dry, at the tremendous cost at the time of £1 million.

The **United Arab Emirates** (**UAE**),[[b]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-15) also known simply as the **Emirates**,[[c]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-16) is a country in [West Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Asia "West Asia"), situated at the eastern end of the [Arabian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula "Arabian Peninsula"). It is a [federal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_monarchy "Federal monarchy") semi-constitutional [monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy "Monarchy") made up of [seven emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirates_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "Emirates of the United Arab Emirates"), with [Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi") serving as its national capital. The UAE borders [Oman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oman "Oman") to the east and northeast, and [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") to the south and southwest. It shares [maritime borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_boundary "Maritime boundary") with Saudi Arabia, [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar"), and [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") in the [Persian Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf"), and with Oman in the [Gulf of Oman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Oman "Gulf of Oman"). In 2024, the UAE had an estimated population of over 11 million. [Dubai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai "Dubai") is the country's [largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_the_United_Arab_Emirates "List of cities in the United Arab Emirates"). [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") is the [state religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_religion "State religion"). [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic "Arabic") is the official language while [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") remains the most spoken language and the language of business.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-Siemund-2)[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-17)

The present-day United Arab Emirates is located within the historical region of [Eastern Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Arabia "Eastern Arabia"), which was oriented to [maritime trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_trade "Maritime trade") and [seafaring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seafaring "Seafaring"). The [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire") arrived in the region around 1500 and set up bases on the territory while waging [wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese%E2%80%93Safavid_wars "Portuguese–Safavid wars") against the [Persians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safavid_Iran "Safavid Iran"). By the 19th century, with [pearling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearling_industry "Pearling industry") becoming a major economic activity, [piracy became rampant in the gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piracy_in_the_Persian_Gulf "Piracy in the Persian Gulf"), prompting [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") intervention.[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-bandits-18)[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-:11-19) Local [sheikhdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikhdoms "Sheikhdoms") formed a pact with the United Kingdom to create the [Trucial States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trucial_States "Trucial States"), a [British protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_protectorate "British protectorate") that was effectively shielded from attempted [Saudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Saudi_state "First Saudi state") and [Omani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omani_Empire "Omani Empire")[suzerainty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzerainty "Suzerainty").[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-20) The Trucial States remained under British influence until full independence as the United Arab Emirates in 1971. [Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_bin_Sultan_Al_Nahyan "Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan"), ruler of Abu Dhabi and the country's first president (1971–2004), oversaw rapid development of the Emirates by investing revenues from newly found [oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_reserve "Oil reserve") into [healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_care "Health care"), [education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education "Education"), and [infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure "Infrastructure").[[18]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-21)

The United Arab Emirates is considered a [middle power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_power "Middle power") in global affairs;[[19]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-22) Dubai serves as an international hub of finance, tourism, and commerce.[[20]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-:9-23)[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-24) Only 11% of the population are native [Emiratis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emiratis "Emiratis"); the vast majority of inhabitants are [expatriates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expatriates "Expatriates") and [migrant workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migrant_workers "Migrant workers"), most of whom are from [South Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia").[[22]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-25) The UAE has the world's [seventh-largest oil reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_proven_oil_reserves "List of countries by proven oil reserves") and [seventh-largest natural gas reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_natural_gas_proven_reserves "List of countries by natural gas proven reserves").[[23]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-EIA-26)[[24]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-27) The UAE has the most diversified economy among the members of the [Gulf Cooperation Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Cooperation_Council "Gulf Cooperation Council") (GCC), having become less reliant on natural resources in the 21st century and increasingly focusing on tourism and business.[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-28) The UAE is a member of the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations"), [Arab League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_League "Arab League"), [Organisation of Islamic Cooperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_Islamic_Cooperation "Organisation of Islamic Cooperation"), [Non-Aligned Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement "Non-Aligned Movement"), [World Trade Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Organization "World Trade Organization"), and [BRICS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRICS "BRICS"); it is also a dialogue partner of the [Shanghai Cooperation Organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Cooperation_Organisation "Shanghai Cooperation Organisation").

The [Federal Supreme Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Supreme_Council "Federal Supreme Council"), made up of the seven ruling [emirs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirs "Emirs"), is the highest state authority. It jointly appoints one member as [federal president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "President of the United Arab Emirates"), who appoints a [prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_prime_ministers_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "List of prime ministers of the United Arab Emirates"), who forms and leads [the cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "Cabinet of the United Arab Emirates").[[26]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-29) The UAE is an [authoritarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarianism "Authoritarianism") state but generally liberal by regional standards.[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-:11-19) It ranks highly in several social indicators such as housing, [healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_the_United_Arab_Emirates "Healthcare in the United Arab Emirates"), [education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_the_United_Arab_Emirates "Education in the United Arab Emirates") and personal safety, as well as the highest regionally in the [Human Development Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Development_Index "Human Development Index").[[27]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-30) Human rights organisations consider the UAE substandard on human rights, ranking low in the [human freedom index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Freedom_Index "Human Freedom Index") due to reports of government critics being imprisoned and tortured, families harassed by the state security apparatus, and cases of [forced disappearances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_disappearance "Forced disappearance").[[28]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-31) Individual rights such as the freedoms of [assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_assembly "Freedom of assembly"), [association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_association "Freedom of association"), [expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_expression "Freedom of expression"), and the [freedom of the press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Press_Freedom_Index "Press Freedom Index") are severely repressed.[[29]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-32)

## Etymology

The United Arab Emirates is named after the seven emirates that formed a federation: the Emirate of [Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi"), the Emirate of [Dubai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai "Dubai"), the Emirate of [Ajman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajman "Ajman"), the Emirate of [Sharjah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharjah "Sharjah"), the Emirate of [Ras Al Khaimah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah "Ras Al Khaimah"), the Emirate of [Umm Al Quwain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umm_Al_Quwain "Umm Al Quwain"), and the Emirate of [Fujairah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujairah "Fujairah").[[30]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-33)

## History

Main article: [History of the United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "History of the United Arab Emirates")

### Antiquity

[![Image 15](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/C%C3%A1ntaro_%2826738115330%29.jpg/250px-C%C3%A1ntaro_%2826738115330%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:C%C3%A1ntaro_(26738115330).jpg)

2nd century [BCE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era "Common Era") era jar found in [Mleiha Archaeological site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mleiha_Archaeological_Centre "Mleiha Archaeological Centre") in Sharjah

Stone tools recovered reveal a settlement of people from Africa some 127,000 years ago and a stone tool used for butchering animals discovered on the Arabian coast suggests an even older habitation from 130,000 years ago.[[31]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-34) In time, lively trading links developed with civilisations in [Mesopotamia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesopotamia "Mesopotamia"), Iran, and the [Harappan culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_Valley_civilisation "Indus Valley civilisation") of the Indus Valley. This contact persisted and became wider, probably motivated by the trade in copper from the [Hajar Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajar_Mountains "Hajar Mountains"), which commenced around 3,000 BCE.[[32]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-35) Sumerian sources talk of the [Magan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magan_(civilization) "Magan (civilization)") civilisation, which has been identified as encompassing the modern UAE and Oman.[[33]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-36)

There are six periods of human settlement with distinctive behaviours in the region before Islam, which include the [Hafit period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafit_period "Hafit period") from 3,200 to 2,600 BCE, the [Umm Al Nar culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umm_Al_Nar_culture "Umm Al Nar culture") from 2,600 to 2,000 BCE, and the [Wadi Suq culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wadi_Suq_culture "Wadi Suq culture") from 2,000 to 1,300 BCE. From 1,200 BCE to the advent of Islam in Eastern Arabia, through three distinctive [Iron Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age_in_the_United_Arab_Emirates "Iron Age in the United Arab Emirates") and the [Mleiha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mleiha "Mleiha") period, the area was variously occupied by the [Achaemenids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire "Achaemenid Empire") and other forces, and saw the construction of fortified settlements and extensive husbandry thanks to the development of the [_falaj_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qanat "Qanat") irrigation system.

### Islam

The spread of [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") to the northeastern tip of the [Arabian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula "Arabian Peninsula") is thought to have followed directly from a letter sent by the [Islamic prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_prophet "Islamic prophet")[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") to the rulers of [Oman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oman "Oman") in 630 CE. This led to a group of rulers travelling to [Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina "Medina"), converting to Islam, and subsequently driving a successful uprising against the unpopular [Sassanids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasanian_Empire "Sasanian Empire"), who dominated the coast at the time.[[34]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeard-Bey1996127-37) Following the death of Muhammad, the new Islamic communities south of the [Persian Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf") threatened to disintegrate, with insurrections against the [Muslim leaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_leaders "Muslim leaders"). Caliph [Abu Bakr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Bakr "Abu Bakr") sent an army from the capital Medina which completed its reconquest of the territory ([the Ridda Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridda_wars "Ridda wars")) with the [Battle of Dibba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dibba "Battle of Dibba") in which 10,000 lives are thought to have been lost.[[35]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeard-Bey1996127%E2%80%93128-38) This assured the integrity of the [Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate "Caliphate") and the unification of the Arabian Peninsula under the newly emerging [Rashidun Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashidun_Caliphate "Rashidun Caliphate").

In 637, Julfar—situated within the geographic boundaries of modern-day [Ras Al Khaimah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah "Ras Al Khaimah")—was an important port that was used as a staging post for the Islamic invasion of the [Sasanian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasanian_Empire "Sasanian Empire").[[36]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-AbedHellyer2001-39) The area of the [Al Ain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Ain "Al Ain")/[Buraimi Oasis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buraimi_Oasis "Buraimi Oasis") was known as Tu'am and was an important trading post for camel routes between the coast and the Arabian interior.[[37]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeard-Bey199622%E2%80%9323-40)

The earliest [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") site in the UAE was first discovered in the 1990s, an extensive monastic complex on what is now known as [Sir Bani Yas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Bani_Yas "Sir Bani Yas") Island and which dates back to the seventh century. Thought to be [Nestorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nestorianism "Nestorianism") and built in 600 CE, the church appears to have been abandoned peacefully in 750 CE.[[38]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-41) It forms a rare physical link to a legacy of Christianity, which is thought to have spread across the peninsula from 50 to 350 CE following trade routes. Certainly, by the fifth century, Oman had a bishop named John – the last bishop of Oman being Etienne, in 676 CE.[[39]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-42)

### Portuguese era

See also: [Battle of the Strait of Hormuz (1553)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Strait_of_Hormuz_(1553) "Battle of the Strait of Hormuz (1553)") and [Piracy in the Persian Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piracy_in_the_Persian_Gulf "Piracy in the Persian Gulf")

[![Image 16](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Forte_de_doba.jpg/250px-Forte_de_doba.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Forte_de_doba.jpg)

A painting of the [Portuguese Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire")[Doba Fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doba_Fortress?action=edit&redlink=1 "Doba Fortress (page does not exist)")[[pt](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forte%20de%20Doba "pt:Forte de Doba")] in [Dibba Al-Hisn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dibba_Al-Hisn "Dibba Al-Hisn") in 1620

The harsh desert environment led to the emergence of the "versatile tribesman", nomadic groups who subsisted due to a variety of economic activities, including animal husbandry, agriculture, and hunting. The seasonal movements of these groups led not only to frequent clashes between groups but also to the establishment of seasonal and semi-seasonal settlements and centres. These formed tribal groupings whose names are still carried by modern Emiratis, including the [Bani Yas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bani_Yas "Bani Yas") and [Al Bu Falah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Nahyan_family "Al Nahyan family") of [Abu Dhabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi"), Al Ain, [Liwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liwa_Oasis "Liwa Oasis"), and the west coast; the [Dhawahir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhawahir "Dhawahir"), Awamir, [Al Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Ali_(tribe) "Al Ali (tribe)"), and [Manasir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manasir_(tribe) "Manasir (tribe)") of the interior; the [Sharqiyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharqiyin "Sharqiyin") of the east coast; and the [Qawasim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qasimi "Al-Qasimi") to the north.[[40]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-43)

With the expansion of European [colonial empires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_empire "Colonial empire"), [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire"), [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire"), and [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Empire "Dutch Empire") forces appeared in the Persian Gulf region. By the 18th century, the Bani Yas confederation was the dominant force in most of the area now known as Abu Dhabi,[[41]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeard-Bey199643-44)[[42]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-45)[[43]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-46) while the Northern [Al Qawasim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qasimi "Al-Qasimi") (Al Qasimi) dominated maritime commerce. The Portuguese maintained an influence over the coastal settlements, building [forts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortification "Fortification") in the wake of the bloody 16th-century conquests of coastal communities by [Albuquerque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque "Afonso de Albuquerque") and the Portuguese commanders who followed him – particularly on the east coast at [Muscat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscat "Muscat"), [Sohar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sohar "Sohar"), and [Khor Fakkan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khor_Fakkan "Khor Fakkan").[[44]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeard-Bey1996282-47)

The southern coast of the Persian Gulf was known to the British as the "[Pirate Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "History of the United Arab Emirates")",[[45]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-48)[[46]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-49) as boats of the Al Qawasim federation harassed British-flagged shipping from the 17th century into the 19th.[[47]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-50) The charge of piracy is disputed by modern Emirati historians, including the current ruler of Sharjah, [Sheikh Sultan Al Qasimi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_bin_Muhammad_Al-Qasimi "Sultan bin Muhammad Al-Qasimi"), in his 1986 book _The Myth of Arab Piracy in the Gulf_.[[48]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-51)

[![Image 17](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Persian_Gulf_1507-1750.gif/250px-Persian_Gulf_1507-1750.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Persian_Gulf_1507-1750.gif)

Purple – [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire") in the Persian Gulf in the 16th and 17th century. Main cities, ports, and routes.

[![Image 18](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Ras_Al_Khaimah_under_attack%2C_1809_01.jpg/250px-Ras_Al_Khaimah_under_attack%2C_1809_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ras_Al_Khaimah_under_attack,_1809_01.jpg)

A painting depicting the burning of the coastal town and port of [Emirate of Ras Al Khaimah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Ras_Al_Khaimah "Emirate of Ras Al Khaimah") during the [Persian Gulf campaign of 1809](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf_campaign_of_1809 "Persian Gulf campaign of 1809")

British expeditions to protect their Indian trade routes led to campaigns against Ras Al Khaimah and other harbours along the coast, including the [Persian Gulf campaign of 1809](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf_campaign_of_1809 "Persian Gulf campaign of 1809") and the more successful [campaign of 1819](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf_campaign_of_1819 "Persian Gulf campaign of 1819"). The following year, Britain and a number of local rulers signed a [maritime truce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Maritime_Treaty_of_1820 "General Maritime Treaty of 1820"),[[49]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-52) giving rise to the term [Trucial States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trucial_States "Trucial States"), which came to define the status of the coastal emirates. A further treaty was signed in 1843 and in 1853, the [Perpetual Maritime Truce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetual_Maritime_Truce "Perpetual Maritime Truce") was agreed. To this was added the 'Exclusive Agreements', signed in 1892, which made the Trucial States a British protectorate.[[50]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-53)

Under the 1892 treaty, the trucial sheikhs agreed not to dispose of any territory except to the British and not to enter into relationships with any foreign government other than the British without their consent. In return, the British promised to protect the Trucial Coast from all aggression by sea and to help in case of land attack. British maritime policing meant that pearling fleets could operate in relative security. However, the British prohibition of the [slave trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_slavery "History of slavery") meant an important source of income was lost to some sheikhs and merchants.[[51]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-54)

In 1869, the Qubaisat tribe settled at [Khor Al Adaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khor_Al_Adaid "Khor Al Adaid") and tried to enlist the support of the Ottomans. Khor Al Adaid was claimed by Abu Dhabi at that time, a claim supported by the British. In 1906, the British Political Resident, [Percy Cox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Cox "Percy Cox"), confirmed in writing to the ruler of Abu Dhabi, [Zayed bin Khalifa Al Nahyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_bin_Khalifa_Al_Nahyan "Zayed bin Khalifa Al Nahyan") ('Zayed the Great'), that Khor Al Adaid belonged to his sheikhdom.[[52]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-55)

### British era and discovery of oil

See also: [Persian Gulf campaign of 1809](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf_campaign_of_1809 "Persian Gulf campaign of 1809"), [Persian Gulf campaign of 1819](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf_campaign_of_1819 "Persian Gulf campaign of 1819"), [General Maritime Treaty of 1820](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Maritime_Treaty_of_1820 "General Maritime Treaty of 1820"), and [Trucial States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trucial_States "Trucial States")

[![Image 19](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Dhayah_Fort_showing_hilltop_location.jpg/250px-Dhayah_Fort_showing_hilltop_location.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dhayah_Fort_showing_hilltop_location.jpg)

[Dhayah Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhayah_Fort "Dhayah Fort") at the hill top. In 1819 it was the last [Al-Qasimi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qasimi "Al-Qasimi") stronghold to fall in the [Persian Gulf campaign of 1819](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf_campaign_of_1819 "Persian Gulf campaign of 1819"). The fall of Dhayah was to pave the way for the signing of the [General Maritime Treaty of 1820](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Maritime_Treaty_of_1820 "General Maritime Treaty of 1820").

During the 19th and early 20th centuries, the [pearling industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_hunting "Pearl hunting") thrived, providing both income and employment to the people of the Persian Gulf.[[53]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-56) The [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") had a severe impact on the industry, but it was the [economic depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_depression "Economic depression") of the late 1920s and early 1930s, coupled with the invention of the [cultured pearl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultured_pearl "Cultured pearl"), that wiped out the trade. The remnants of the trade eventually faded away shortly after the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), when the newly independent [Government of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India "Government of India") imposed heavy taxation on imported pearls. The decline of pearling resulted in extreme economic hardship in the Trucial States.[[54]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-57)

In 1922, the British government secured undertakings from the rulers of the Trucial States not to sign concessions with foreign companies without their consent. Aware of the potential for the development of natural resources such as oil, following finds in Persia (from 1908) and Mesopotamia (from 1927), a British-led oil company, the [Iraq Petroleum Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_Petroleum_Company "Iraq Petroleum Company") (IPC), showed an interest in the region. The [Anglo-Persian Oil Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Persian_Oil_Company "Anglo-Persian Oil Company") (APOC, later to become [British Petroleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BP "BP"), or BP) had a 23.75% share in IPC. From 1935, onshore concessions to explore for oil were granted by local rulers, with APOC signing the first one on behalf of Petroleum Concessions Ltd (PCL), an associate company of IPC.[[55]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates#cite_note-58)

APOC was prevented from developing the region alone because of the restrictions of the [Red Line Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_Agreement "Red Line Agreement"), which required it to operate through IPC. The United Arab Emirates (UAE),[b] also known simply as the Emirates,[c] is a country in West Asia, situated at the eastern end of the Arabian Peninsula. It is a federal semi-constitutional monarchy made up of seven emirates, with Abu Dhabi serving as its national capital. The UAE borders Oman to the east and northeast, and Saudi Arabia to the south and southwest. It shares maritime borders with Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Iran in the Persian Gulf, and with Oman in the Gulf of Oman. In 2024, the UAE had an estimated population of over 11 million. Dubai is the country's largest city. Islam is the state religion. Arabic is the official language while English remains the most spoken language and the language of business.[2][14]

The present-day United Arab Emirates is located within the historical region of Eastern Arabia, which was oriented to maritime trade and seafaring. The Portuguese arrived in the region around 1500 and set up bases on the territory while waging wars against the Persians. By the 19th century, with pearling becoming a major economic activity, piracy became rampant in the gulf, prompting British intervention.[15][16] Local sheikhdoms formed a pact with the United Kingdom to create the Trucial States, a British protectorate that was effectively shielded from attempted Saudi and Omani suzerainty.[17] The Trucial States remained under British influence until full independence as the United Arab Emirates in 1971. Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, ruler of Abu Dhabi and the country's first president (1971–2004), oversaw rapid development of the Emirates by investing revenues from newly found oil into healthcare, education, and infrastructure.[18]

The United Arab Emirates is considered a middle power in global affairs;[19] Dubai serves as an international hub of finance, tourism, and commerce.[20][21] Only 11% of the population are native Emiratis; the vast majority of inhabitants are expatriates and migrant workers, most of whom are from South Asia.[22] The UAE has the world's seventh-largest oil reserves and seventh-largest natural gas reserves.[23][24] The UAE has the most diversified economy among the members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), having become less reliant on natural resources in the 21st century and increasingly focusing on tourism and business.[25] The UAE is a member of the United Nations, Arab League, Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, Non-Aligned Movement, World Trade Organization, and BRICS; it is also a dialogue partner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.

The Federal Supreme Council, made up of the seven ruling emirs, is the highest state authority. It jointly appoints one member as federal president, who appoints a prime minister, who forms and leads the cabinet.[26] The UAE is an authoritarian state but generally liberal by regional standards.[16] It ranks highly in several social indicators such as housing, healthcare, education and personal safety, as well as the highest regionally in the Human Development Index.[27] Human rights organisations consider the UAE substandard on human rights, ranking low in the human freedom index due to reports of government critics being imprisoned and tortured, families harassed by the state security apparatus, and cases of forced disappearances.[28] Individual rights such as the freedoms of assembly, association, expression, and the freedom of the press are severely repressed.[29]

Etymology

The United Arab Emirates is named after the seven emirates that formed a federation: the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, the Emirate of Dubai, the Emirate of Ajman, the Emirate of Sharjah, the Emirate of Ras Al Khaimah, the Emirate of Umm Al Quwain, and the Emirate of Fujairah.[30]

History
Main article: History of the United Arab Emirates
Antiquity
2nd century BCE era jar found in Mleiha Archaeological site in Sharjah

Stone tools recovered reveal a settlement of people from Africa some 127,000 years ago and a stone tool used for butchering animals discovered on the Arabian coast suggests an even older habitation from 130,000 years ago.[31] In time, lively trading links developed with civilisations in Mesopotamia, Iran, and the Harappan culture of the Indus Valley. This contact persisted and became wider, probably motivated by the trade in copper from the Hajar Mountains, which commenced around 3,000 BCE.[32] Sumerian sources talk of the Magan civilisation, which has been identified as encompassing the modern UAE and Oman.[33]

There are six periods of human settlement with distinctive behaviours in the region before Islam, which include the Hafit period from 3,200 to 2,600 BCE, the Umm Al Nar culture from 2,600 to 2,000 BCE, and the Wadi Suq culture from 2,000 to 1,300 BCE. From 1,200 BCE to the advent of Islam in Eastern Arabia, through three distinctive Iron Ages and the Mleiha period, the area was variously occupied by the Achaemenids and other forces, and saw the construction of fortified settlements and extensive husbandry thanks to the development of the falaj irrigation system.

Islam

The spread of Islam to the northeastern tip of the Arabian Peninsula is thought to have followed directly from a letter sent by the Islamic prophet Muhammad to the rulers of Oman in 630 CE. This led to a group of rulers travelling to Medina, converting to Islam, and subsequently driving a successful uprising against the unpopular Sassanids, who dominated the coast at the time.[34] Following the death of Muhammad, the new Islamic communities south of the Persian Gulf threatened to disintegrate, with insurrections against the Muslim leaders. Caliph Abu Bakr sent an army from the capital Medina which completed its reconquest of the territory (the Ridda Wars) with the Battle of Dibba in which 10,000 lives are thought to have been lost.[35] This assured the integrity of the Caliphate and the unification of the Arabian Peninsula under the newly emerging Rashidun Caliphate.

In 637, Julfar—situated within the geographic boundaries of modern-day Ras Al Khaimah—was an important port that was used as a staging post for the Islamic invasion of the Sasanian Empire.[36] The area of the Al Ain/Buraimi Oasis was known as Tu'am and was an important trading post for camel routes between the coast and the Arabian interior.[37]

The earliest Christian site in the UAE was first discovered in the 1990s, an extensive monastic complex on what is now known as Sir Bani Yas Island and which dates back to the seventh century. Thought to be Nestorian and built in 600 CE, the church appears to have been abandoned peacefully in 750 CE.[38] It forms a rare physical link to a legacy of Christianity, which is thought to have spread across the peninsula from 50 to 350 CE following trade routes. Certainly, by the fifth century, Oman had a bishop named John – the last bishop of Oman being Etienne, in 676 CE.[39]

Portuguese era
See also: Battle of the Strait of Hormuz (1553) and Piracy in the Persian Gulf
A painting of the Portuguese Empire Doba Fortress [pt] in Dibba Al-Hisn in 1620

The harsh desert environment led to the emergence of the "versatile tribesman", nomadic groups who subsisted due to a variety of economic activities, including animal husbandry, agriculture, and hunting. The seasonal movements of these groups led not only to frequent clashes between groups but also to the establishment of seasonal and semi-seasonal settlements and centres. These formed tribal groupings whose names are still carried by modern Emiratis, including the Bani Yas and Al Bu Falah of Abu Dhabi, Al Ain, Liwa, and the west coast; the Dhawahir, Awamir, Al Ali, and Manasir of the interior; the Sharqiyin of the east coast; and the Qawasim to the north.[40]

With the expansion of European colonial empires, Portuguese, English, and Dutch forces appeared in the Persian Gulf region. By the 18th century, the Bani Yas confederation was the dominant force in most of the area now known as Abu Dhabi,[41][42][43] while the Northern Al Qawasim (Al Qasimi) dominated maritime commerce. The Portuguese maintained an influence over the coastal settlements, building forts in the wake of the bloody 16th-century conquests of coastal communities by Albuquerque and the Portuguese commanders who followed him – particularly on the east coast at Muscat, Sohar, and Khor Fakkan.[44]

The southern coast of the Persian Gulf was known to the British as the "Pirate Coast",[45][46] as boats of the Al Qawasim federation harassed British-flagged shipping from the 17th century into the 19th.[47] The charge of piracy is disputed by modern Emirati historians, including the current ruler of Sharjah, Sheikh Sultan Al Qasimi, in his 1986 book The Myth of Arab Piracy in the Gulf.[48]
